utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I call upon the registrar to call the case. I wonder whether we could start with the video conference. I assume the first witness will be Zivko Licina. Mr. Bos, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Very soft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Should I speak louder?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we can start. Could you ask the witness to stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila? ZIVKO LICINA, Sworn:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, did you make a statement to Investigator Vojislav Ore and could you please take a look at it and say whether this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, what are you by profession and where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a professor of mathematics. I worked in the Vukovar High School before the war, and I still work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Emil Cakalic or Dragutin Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never met them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, could you remember the following date, the 20th of November, 1991 now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was happening to you on that day, how come you were at the hospital, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to the hospital on the 2nd of November, 1991, together with my wife who fell ill in the cellar where we were staying in Mitnica. Due to my wife's illness, I stayed on at the hospital too until the war operations had ceased on the 20th of November. On that day, we left the hospital, my wife and I, in a bus around 11.00. We arrived in Ovcara sometime between 1.00 and 1.30 p.m. We spent some time there and, at one point in time, a soldier came by (redacted) who recognised me and my wife on the bus, and who asked us to leave the bus immediately, which is exactly what we did. (redacted) recognised --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the name

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- recognised someone, and they -- so it's a few people, left the bus too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, there is no tone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in front of the bus, we went to the command of the military unit which was near the buses -- near the place where the buses were. We stayed there all afternoon and sometime around dusk we were taken to VELEPROMET. We were driven off to VELEPROMET. We spent the night at VELEPROMET and the next day, on the 21st of November, we left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, do you remember in which bus you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many buses were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many buses were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus was full, but we were all sitting. We all had seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you left the bus, did you leave this place immediately or did you spend some time in front of the hanger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent a few minutes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you see him, had he been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I certainly would have seen him had he been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you were leaving Ovcara, what time was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dusk. Perhaps around 5.00, 4.30 or 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Slavko Dokmanovic certainly was not at the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who drove you away from there then and who were you with in this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military vehicle. I didn't see the driver. I think it was a Jeep. The four of us sat there (redacted), we sat in this vehicle, and then we went to -- back to VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you talk about something en route, how you left Ovcara? Was there any discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the car, really. There wasn't any special conversation because all afternoon the four of us were together in the command of this military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, finally, am I saying the truth when I say that you arrived in front of the hangar between 1.30 and 2.00, and you left the area sometime before 5.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that would be it. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you for coming. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williamson? CROSS-EXAMINED BY MR. WILLIAMSON:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Licina. Do you remember meeting with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Vladimir Dzuro, on the 16th and 17th of November, 1997 in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time did you give him a statement that was taken down in the English language but was read back to you in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And after having the statement read back to you by the interpreter, did you, in fact, sign it as being truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that the witness be shown a copy of the statement which we will mark as the next Prosecutor's exhibit number, if the registrar could help me there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is number D101.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, this is a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Williamson. I forgot to ask for our statement to be admitted into evidence, if you don't object to that. I'm sorry. And I haven't even seen your statement, so could I please have a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the Defence Exhibit being entered, and at this time that's what I was preparing to do, was to hand over our copy. I was just trying to mark it for identification purposes before doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The name, perhaps, the name should be deleted. Your Honour, the witness, Licina, mentioned a name.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So if I could have the Prosecutor's exhibit number, please, the next one in line?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is number 204.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time I would ask if a copy of this could be shown to the witness, and I will provide now copies both in English and Serbian to the Defence and to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The witness has a copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Professor Licina, is this your signature that appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's no signature here. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 204 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Professor Licina, you are a Serb, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you are originally from Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born near Prodavska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long had you lived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And where was your home located in Vukovar in 1991, in what part of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are familiar with Vukovar, it was Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the area that is located near the water tower, is it not, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what were conditions like in Mitnica during the course of the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what conditions you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were your living conditions like during this time period, for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean during the fighting? You mean during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my wife and I lived in the basement until we went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you forced to stay at your home during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that I was forced by someone, but it's a pity I hadn't left before the fighting began.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware of other Serbs that also chose to stay in Vukovar during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them remained. I can't say how many, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, at any time during the battle, while you were staying at your home in Mitnica, were you mistreated by the Croats because you were a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not especially because of that. There wasn't any mistreatment because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened to Mitnica during the course of the battle? Did the area sustain much damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did this damage come from artillery or air attacks or a combination of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was difficult for me to see what was going on up there from my basement and to see where the shelling was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that, on the 2nd of November, you moved to Vukovar Hospital because your wife fell ill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how did you get from your home to the hospital on the 2nd of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a neighbour drove me in his car, me and my wife I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was this neighbour a Croatian soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember right now whether he was a soldier or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to Mr. Ore, you said on the 2nd of November, "One of my neighbours found a Croatian soldier who agreed to drive us to the hospital. I do not know his name." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that he was a soldier, and it is for certain that my neighbour found this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And while you were at the hospital, were you ever mistreated in any way because you were a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say that I was mistreated, no, in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There were a lot of allegations made to the effect that the medical staff at Vukovar Hospital was mistreating Serbs. Did you ever see any evidence of this in the 18 days that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any evidence of that kind where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Mr. Williamson, but I never claimed, nor did anyone here, that Serbs were mistreated at the Vukovar Hospital. I don't know who said that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there have been allegations to that effect. I think the transcript is very clear on that during the course of the trial, that this has come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Serb doctors were there. Serb doctors were there. How come? Which one of the witnesses for the Defence said that he or she was mistreated there? Show me the transcript. Not a single Defence witness has been speaking of the hospital, by the way. I mean, I don't mind if somebody had testified to that, but as far as I know, no one had testified to that effect. It would have been terrible had it been so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This was the last question I had on this topic, but Witness Q testified to this effect, that Dr. Bosanac was looked at as a Dr. Mengele by the Serbs taken to the hospital. She was also taken and imprisoned after the hospital was taken over, as were other members of the hospital staff by the Serb authorities. They were imprisoned in Serbia on allegations for war crimes, that they had taken blood from the prisoners. This has come out due to testimony of Dr. Bosanac, from Dr. Striber and from Witness Q, and I'm addressing this to a Serb who was present in the hospital and asking him: Did he see any evidence of this? But as I said, this was my last question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the night between the 19th and the 20th of November, where were you located in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same part where I had spent the previous 17 or 18 days; namely, in the basement of the neuropsychiatry ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And approximately what time on the morning of the 20th were you directed outside of the hospital and told to get on buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was around 9.00 when we were told to leave, and then it took time. I mean, when we left and while the buses got there, et cetera, so it did take quite a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the buses -- were you able to tell what kind of licence plates were on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't remember the numbers, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But were these licence plates of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I think they were JNA. I can't say that for sure right now, but I think they were JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you got on the bus, was there any type of military personnel on the bus with you and your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a soldier there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when you got on the bus, where did you think you were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to get to Novi Sad as soon as possible, and that is what I thought, that I was going to Novi Sad. I was naive, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, after the buses left the hospital, they did not go directly to Ovcara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. They didn't go immediately. As I said a few minutes ago, we arrived at Ovcara around 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So where did you stop in between?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we stopped -- I can't say this for sure now -- but I think it was the economic yard of Vupik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that is located adjacent to the JNA barracks, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nearby, yes, near the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we left around 11.00 and if we arrived around 1.30, then it is possible that we stayed there for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And while you were there at this place where the buses were parked, at some point in time did a former student of yours, who was a soldier, spot you on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did the soldier seem upset that you were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was surprised to see me there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he make any attempts to get you off of the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did try. I think he tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he, in fact, get on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did another soldier get on the bus and speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the end, you were not taken off the bus at this location, though, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When the buses left from there, did they go directly to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Ovcara, what did you observe occurring there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We didn't pay attention. Quite simply, I didn't pay attention because I was waiting for the buses to go on. I didn't know where we were located. I think, as I said a moment ago, that we were going towards Novi Sad. Until the soldier turned up, who recognised us, asked us to leave the bus, and, as I said a moment ago, took us to the command of that military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many people did this soldier take off the bus there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, my wife, myself, and two others, two other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, your wife is of Czech ethnicity; is she not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the soldier seem concerned about the reaction of the other Serb soldiers if he took more people off of the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know how far he was concerned. That's his own personal affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, do you recall telling Mr. Dzuro in the statement, "He said that if he made any mistakes, they would kill him"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't quite remember that now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, would you like to read the part of the statement where that is indicated? It's on page 5 of the English version. I'm not sure exactly where the Serb version, where that would be, but it begins the paragraph with: "As soldier B took the other two men from the bus, I saw other people trying to attract his attention. Obviously desperate to get out as well." This would be probably the next-to-the-last page, or perhaps the third-from-the-last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you said "Soldier B was in a very bad state because he could not afford to make mistakes. He said that he was sure that the four of us did nothing wrong, but that even as he knew those others, he could not guarantee for them. He said that if he made any mistakes, they would kill him. He did not specify who those "they" were, but I assumed he meant his fellow soldiers." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said something along those lines. He said that he couldn't be certain of all of them to take them out from the bus, and I don't know upon whose suggestion he did take us off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that when you got off the bus, you were able to see a little more clearly about what was happening there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say again that I did not pay attention to what was happening around the bus, towards that particular part, but what I did say I have already stated -- see, I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you were able to see what was going on in front of the hangar, were you not, that people were being taken off the bus and going through a line of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, I say that I did not pay attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So were you able to see the people that were standing in front of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, let me say that I did not recognise anybody, and I was not paying a great deal of attention to what was happening, as you say, with that line, line of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph just above the one that I asked you to look at, the last couple of sentences, you indicate that, "The first bus and our bus were a few metres apart, so I would say that I must have been at least 40 metres away from the soldiers. Since I wear glasses, it was impossible for me to recognise anyone in that group, either the soldiers or the people climbing down from the first bus." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "more or less"? Was it possible for you to recognise anyone in front of the building, anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was possible, but I just looked for a second. I glanced there for a second and saw that I didn't recognise anybody and continued to talk to the people that were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you the number. I really can't tell you how many. After seven years, it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In uniforms and civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult under those conditions to say what a uniform was and what civilian clothing was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But I assume that it would be fair to say that you looked for just a second, from approximately 40 metres away, did not recognise anyone there, and turned the other direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, after this, this soldier that had taken you off the bus, did he take you to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He took us to the command of a military unit close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicated that this was a yellow building about 150 to 200 metres back from where the buses were parked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's roughly right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you went into this yellow building, did you have the opportunity to speak to a JNA officer who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with this JNA officer? I believe in your statement you said that he was a Captain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I think he was, but the military ranks in war, I'm not sure that I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did you have discussions with this officer in regard to the shelling of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And do you recall what was said during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember that he asked -- we said we were going from the hospital, and he said, "How come the hospital was shelled all the time?" "No", he said, "we are aiming at military objects."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Based on your conversation with him, did you ascertain that he was affiliated with some type of artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, after all of this happened, you indicated that you went to Serbia. At some point in time, did you return back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After three days, I went back after three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you have remained in Vukovar since that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the Croats who had lived in Vukovar prior to the battle? Were they still in Vukovar when you went back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were not there. Most of them were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have just now seen the statement that he made, but I have no objections, but I'd like to ask a question. It's an unfavourable position that I am in. But never mind, this is not the first time. Re-examined by Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, in the statement you made to Investigator ^ Zira, you talked about shelling from the hospital, that there was firing from the hospital, but you don't know whether it was from the hospital or from the environs of the hospital. What do you mean by the environs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The courtyard. Well, it's difficult for me to say because I was in the basement of the hospital, so whether -- how far away this was, from whence the firing came, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now a final question for you, Mr. Licina. You wear glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you were 40 metres away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that for a short time you remained in front of the hospital -- in front of the hangar, I'm sorry. Did you find these glasses an impediment to seeing Mr. Dokmanovic, if he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not an impediment because I looked, I did not recognise anybody, and I turned in the other direction and continued my conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And let us repeat: When you went back, how far away from the hangar were you then before leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went to this building --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And you came back from the building, and how far away from the hangar were you then? Never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started right out in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you say that Slavko Dokmanovic, when you were in front of Ovcara and looked that way, that he was not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I was, he was certainly not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Licina, I have just one question for you. You mentioned that a soldier -- you said at some point a soldier at Ovcara, a soldier recognised yourself and your wife and asked you to leave the bus. May I ask you whether the soldier, this soldier, was wearing a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a camouflage uniform, and I don't think he had a cap on his head, so that I can't say whether it was the JNA or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Was he wearing any insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much, Professor Licina, for giving evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we move on to our next witness, we want to express some sort of misgivings about the Prosecutor handing a document, a witness statement in court, without previously informing the Defence. And since this is a crucial point, it is not actually regulated in our rules of procedure and evidence, we were wondering whether we could hear argument at some stage, maybe this week, on this particular point, whether or not it is appropriate for a party to produce in court a witness statement before prior information or notification to the other party. So I wonder whether we could now move on. However, as I say, I think we could spend some time arguing this point so that we may eventually make a ruling on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you wish, we can address it right now, if this is an issue that the Court wants to take up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on -- I don't want to hold up the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, all your arguments are quite all right, but let us not waste time because we have a lot of witnesses to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And I can hear your arguments on Wednesday when we don't have the video link, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think it's a good suggestion. Thank you. It's better to put it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And we will go on with the witnesses, so may we -- we are now going to call witness Bakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, Bakic. We have nine witnesses, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Fila, we forgot to give a number to your -- the witness statements of Professor Licina. D101?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 101, yes. I apologise. I forgot. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that same regard, we would mark the Serbian version of Professor Licina's statement as Prosecutor's Exhibit 204A. I believe I only introduced did as 204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakic, good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bakic, what are you by profession and where were you employed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I am a worker by profession and I worked in the Vupik factory of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know Emil Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you, on the 20th of November, 1991, in the afternoon hours, were you at the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were you there? When did you come? What did you come with, and at what time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I drove a combi. I went there with a combi at about half past 4.00, twenty to five p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I was told that I had to take some people from Ovcara to the VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you see Emil Cakalic, if you did see him there?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I saw him in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There is an objection to the transcript. It says 4.00 or 5.00. No? It was half past four, twenty to five. Is that correct? Is that what you said, Mr. Bakic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, half past four, twenty to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the visibility in Ovcara at the time like?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was dusk, half dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you see Emil Cakalic and what did you do when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I saw him and several others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were they standing?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: In front of the door as you get out of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I drove the combi, and then they told me to take the five of them and to take them to VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you leave your combi?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stepped out of the combi.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you stay for some time in front of the Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you at any point around Emil Cakalic or anywhere there, as far as you could see, did you see Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when did you leave Ovcara and who with?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Well, five of them and myself left at around 5.00 p.m. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was in the car with you that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I only know Cakalic was there and Kojic and a boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it Zoric perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right, Kojic. During the drive, did these people tell you how they were released from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Well, during our talk they said that it was difficult but that they recognised Zoric and Stero and that he took them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they say that they recognised anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they mention in their conversation Slavko Dokmanovic, that they had recognised Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you discuss Slavko Dokmanovic at all in the course of your journey?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann? Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I forgot again. Sorry. This is only because I'm in a hurry. I tried to finish this as soon as possible. Excuse me, Mr. Niemann, may I just show him the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement to Miroslav Vasic, an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Show it to me. It's from my office. Is that your statement? Is your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Take a look at it, see if you signed it. This is Miroslav Vasic, a lawyer from my office?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, please admit this into evidence as D102 and the English version would be 102B. And sorry, Mr. Niemann, sorry once again, but we just want to have as many people as possible, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bakic, I just have a few questions for you, if I may? Did you have a military position during the war on Vukovar, that is leading up to the 20th of November, 1991, or was it a civilian job that you had?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, on the day of the 20th of November, who was it that told you that you should go out to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who told me to do that, but I was so told at VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And are you able to say whether the person that told you to do it was wearing a military uniform or was he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And approximately when were you given the order or request or whatever it might be to go out to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell really what time it was. I didn't even look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, you say that you -- I think it's your evidence that you arrived there at about 4.30. It would have taken you how long to get there from VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, half an hour, it depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And let's assume it's, say, half an hour. Did you receive the message some considerable time before you left or did it seem to you, from thinking back now, that it may have been just that you received the request and then you immediately left? Are you able to help me that way?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, what were you told? What was the directions that you were given other than to go to -- go from VELEPROMET to Ovcara? Were you given any other directions?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And they didn't say what they wanted you to do in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the statement that has now been shown to you, the statement that you gave to the investigator for Mr. Fila, you say that -- in the third paragraph of that statement that the Territorial Defence ordered you to go to Ovcara on the 20th of November. Does that refresh your memory as to who it may have been that gave you the order?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Ovcara, did you speak to anyone in particular who was in authority that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I didn't speak to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone speak to you? Did anyone give you any directions or tell you where to park or did it appear that they were expecting you when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I was only told to take those five men to VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who told you to do that; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: A man in uniform, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did he have -- what sort of a uniform did he have on, the man who told you; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did he appear to be a person with any rank, like an officer's status, or was he just an ordinary soldier, or perhaps you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he was -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, were you dressed in military uniform on that day yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you parked your vehicle, you said you got out of the vehicle, did you? It's not what you said in your statement. I think that's something you said just a moment ago, that you got out of your vehicle when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far away from the front of the hangar were you when you got out of your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I was in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far away from the door were you?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: It was at the very door itself. That is where they stood too, the five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's where you collected the five?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, on the way back from Ovcara, you said that they didn't discuss Mr. Dokmanovic. Did they discuss anybody else that was there at Ovcara that day, that is the people you picked up?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: They were just saying that it was very difficult, and they were saying whom they had recognised, and they just mentioned that they recognised Zoric who got them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. So that's the only person they discussed that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you were at Ovcara, did you see any vehicles about, and if so, can you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were the buses parked?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: On the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And were the buses between your vehicle and the entrance to the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: The buses were parked on the road in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any agricultural equipment, such as bulldozers or earth-moving equipment there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers that were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: It was getting dark. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay at Ovcara in all; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Around 15 minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, is the situation this: That you merely parked your vehicle, walked over and collected the five people that were waiting in front of the hangar, and went back to your vehicle and then drove off to VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: MILE BAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? No questions? I assume there is no objection to the witness Bakic being released? Mr. Bakic, thank you for giving evidence. You may be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, now we're going to see who the next witness is. I have no idea, really. Are we going to take a break at 11.00? Stanimirovic. Mr. Bos, could you please call Mr. Stanimirovic? He is short. So I can finish with Mr. Stanimirovic without interfering with the cross. Vodicka, if he is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, could you please tell us the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stanimirovic, could you please stand up and read the formal declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Stanimirovic, did you talk to an investigator from my office, Miroslav Vasic, and did you give him the statement that will be shown to you right now, and do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement. Let me just take a look. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I suggest that this statement be admitted into evidence as D103, and the English version is 103A or B, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Stanimirovic, you completed medical school when and where?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Medicine in Belgrade in 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you employed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I worked throughout my career in Vukovar and, in 1991, I was employed at the Vukovar Hospital as head of ward of psychiatry. I was a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Vukovar after the SDP of (translation unclear) won the elections? We're talking about the period of 1991 when the first multi-party elections were held. What was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The SDP won and the situation was terrible because the HDZ took every kind of initiative and Serbs who were directors of various enterprises were replaced en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a replacement also at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a replacement at the Vukovar Hospital too. This happened on the 25th of July, 1991. I personally know of this case because I was President of the Workers' Council then of the medical centre in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why was the director replaced? Because of his ethnic background or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think he was replaced only because of his ethnic background. This man was director for 16 years. He's a Serb -- a Montenegrin to be very precise. He was replaced by a decree issued by the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Croatia, by Minister Hebrang, and Dr. Vesna Bosanac was appointed acting director.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This Minister Hebrang, who is now the Minister of Military Affairs?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You left Vukovar sometime in July 1991. Could you tell us why you did this?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You see, I first left Vukovar on the 28th of June because I was constantly under pressure. I was receiving telephone calls, my car was stopped two or three times at a time when I was driving through town, so I wanted to take a vacation and I was hoping that the situation would get more peaceful, but this was not the case. The director, until then, Rade Popovic, who was director of the hospital, he called me to Belgrade to come there because I was President of the Workers' Council, and he told me that he was replaced by a decree and that we should have a meeting. He said that Mercep, and the people who were running the city at that point, were not touching doctors and that they wouldn't do anything, so I believed his words and I returned on the 24th of July, in the evening, I came back to Vukovar. The next day, the 25th, we held this meeting of the Workers' Council, we read this decree, and that Workers' Council appointed Dr. Vesna Bosanac acting director of the hospital. And on that day, as I returned home, a synchronised action continued. I was arrested in Vukovar in my apartment and in my family home 25 kilometres away from Vukovar. This happened on the 25th, approximately around 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the reason for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The reason mentioned for my arrest was that I was in Yugoslavia and that I took part in organising the uprising, that they knew that I had weapons, et cetera. However, both searches of my mother's house and of the apartment showed that all of that was untrue. They did not find weapons anywhere except for my pistol, and I had a proper licence for that, and I showed it to them and they took it away from me. After that, they took me to the police station, nevertheless, in Vukovar, where again they interrogated me, what I was doing in Yugoslavia and why did I leave in June, did I know anything about the armament of the Serbs, et cetera. On that evening I was released at the intervention of my wife, and some Croats. I imagine who they were, but I don't know for sure until this very day, but they intervened to have me released from custody, and that is what happened. That evening I spent the night at my neighbour's home, I didn't dare spend the night at my own home, in my own apartment, but there's another thing I didn't mention. When my apartment was being searched, the ZNG practically devastated my mother's house in the village. They broke all the window glasses. They shot at barrels in the basement, in the cellar, where wine and brandy was, so all of it flew out of the barrels. I forgot to mention that. At the police station, after two interrogations, I was advised to leave Vukovar. And that evening, as I said, I spent the night at my neighbour's, and the next day I tried to leave Vukovar, my wife and I tried, without any luggage. We only had our personal documents. However, we did not succeed in doing so because there were barricades at the exit out of Vukovar, so we were taken back to the defence building where practically Mr. Mercep and his deputy, Josip Gazo, were issuing certain certificates or ausweiss. My wife and I were waiting in a queue to get these papers with which we could get out of town. I didn't dare go towards my village. I went to Ilok and I crossed the bridge and went to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. What was Mercep, who was this person, Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You see, for me he was anonymous person. I had never heard of this man until then, but afterwards he was the head commander of the city. His role was far more important than that of the police itself, which did exist there. Perhaps it was fortunate for me, when I was arrested, that the police took me in rather than the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, of Mr. Mercep. These were newly established units, units from the Territorial Defence, probably, they were armed and they were the real power in town. Very often they would take cars without any justification, they would change licence plates, and no one was held accountable to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In addition to yourself, were other Serbs also exposed to that kind of mistreatment like you were?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This happened to all eminent Serbs. That day when I was arrested, my head technician from my ward, his name is Salvo Domanovic (phoen), he was working the third night shift in the hospital, the psychiatry ward, and practically at midnight, at 12.30 a.m. on the 26th, he was taken away from his job at the hospital where he left some 30 patients unprotected. He was taken to his apartment, we think, and his apartment was searched, and all trace was lost of him that day. He was never found until the present day, not even his corpse. And his wife and two children are still in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any cases that Serb shops were looted, burned, that Serbs were beaten up?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were cases of this kind until the 2nd of May. We must point out that until the 2nd of May, until Borovo Selo had happened, not a single Croat had been harmed in Vukovar, but Serb houses, Serb shops, Serb stores, were mined, torched, and I think on the 2nd of May that there were a few murders too. Some other people too, I don't know -- I don't know the names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we say that in addition to you, other eminent Serbs were also leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of the eminent Serbs were leaving Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What percentage could we say? What percentage of the Serb population was leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A large percentage of the Serb population was leaving Vukovar because in Vukovar, it was mostly the elderly people that remained, that is those who were destitute and unprotected. There are very few intellectuals in Vukovar. I can say that in our hospital, out of 30 doctors only four Serb doctors remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is being said here that there was no reason for you to leave, that Serbs were having a wonderful time, a fantastic time there. We have heard from various doctors that they didn't understand why the director of the Vukovar Hospital was replaced. It is being claimed that you did not have a single reason to leave Vukovar. It is even being claimed that you did not leave Vukovar, that the majority stayed, and that they were saying that you were going to football games in Belgrade and that that was later portrayed as a departure, to a departure. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I already said that out of the 30 doctors that were employed that only four Serb doctors remained, so we are not talking about soccer games. The very fact that I was brought into custody, arrested, that I was interrogated and that I was advised in the police station itself that the wisest thing for me to be -- to do would be to leave Vukovar. What they did at my mother's house speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that what they did to the Croats? Was it the Croat police who told you that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The Croat police brought me in for questioning, but the ZNG did this to my mother's house.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear what is being said.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you come back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know Slavko Dokmanovic in the period before you left?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him superficially, not too well, because I was not really involved in politics before the war, but I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, whether he left Vukovar before you did or not? If you don't know, never mind.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slavko Dokmanovic, because of various pressures and closing the entrance into Vukovar at the Trpinja road, I think he left Vukovar already in May and June, but I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. When did you go back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You see, I was coming to Vukovar because I was in charge of the medical corps, but I came back on the 20th of November in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did somebody appoint you civilian director for the renewal of the hospital, and who was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military director and then they appointed me the director for renewal of the hospital. I only dealt in the restoration of the hospital exclusively. I wasn't involved in medical affairs or personnel or anything like that. I didn't have any jurisdiction in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In this period, until the 20th of November, 1991, a few days before that and after that, is it true to say that there was military administration in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. There was certainly military administration in our hospital. In our hospital that was the case until the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in the town of Vukovar itself there were military administration?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many approximately in the town of Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was certainly until the end of the year or the end of December, the beginning of January. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you recall when the first civilian authority was established on the territory of the Municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think this was also at the end of December, the end of the month of December. I can't tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In this period, after the December 1992, did you have certain authority? Were you president of the Municipality of Vukovar or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, you personally.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was President of the Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From when until when?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: For a short period of time until the elections that were held, the multi-party elections, in the former Republic of Srpska Krajina. I think this was the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And who was elected as President of the Municipality at those elections in 1994?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At that time the Radicals won the elections, and I think that the Radical Party appointed Mr. Ljubomir Vukicevic, I think that was his name, from Brsadin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when he was replaced, who came then?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: After he was replaced, Slavko Dokmanovic was appointed. This was actually a coalition of the Serbian Democratic Party, the Socialist Party, and they actually replaced Mr. Vukicevic, and Slavko Dokmanovic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What political post do you hold now in Vukovar and in the Croatian parliament, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about this. During the elections and during the time of Mr. Klein I was the founder of the Independent Serb Party in Croatia and I was President of that party and this party was registered in Croatia. And this party took part in the elections, in the UNTAES period, that is to say during Mr. Klein's time, the time of reintegration. And after that, as party leader, I was proposed by the President of the Republic to be a member of parliament in the Zupanijski Dom, the lower house, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And practically now you are a member of the Croatian parliament and you are president of this party that you mention and you live in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I live in Vukovar with my family and a son of mine is studying in Belgrade now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately in Vukovar, in 1990-91, how many Serbs were there in Vukovar and how many Serbs are there now?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am not very -- are you interested only in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Vukovar and Croatia as a whole, the Municipality of Vukovar and Croatia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to what the current population is. If he wants to talk about the population in 1990 and 1991, which is relevant to the case, that's fine, but to get into the population and statistics in 1998 I think has no relevance to our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the expert witness of the Prosecution, Mr. Wheeler, I think spoke about the population migration from medieval times onwards and he answered questions as to the Serb population now. It is relevant to determine how many there were in 1990 and then the movements up to the present day. This is highly relevant so that we can see the situation as it stands. I have no idea of accusing anybody for this, but just to see the figures, what the figures were and what they are today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just respond very briefly to that? Mr. Wheeler did answer questions on those issues, but those were put to him by Mr. Fila. We did not ask any questions about the period starting from 1945 onward, and all of the questions pertaining to population from medieval periods and in the current times came from Mr. Fila, so he is the one that introduced the issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the basis of the written report by Mr. Wheeler. I said something about that in my introduction, and that is why I wanted these additional explanations. So how many Serbs in 1990 on Croatian territory existed and in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The court feels that the question is not relevant, the question about the population, breakdown of the population --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The composition of the population in 1990 and 1991, that was an important question, and Mr. Williamson asked one of the directors, Witness D, who is not an expert in that matter at all, but he is a politician and can therefore answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the relationship of the population structure in 1990 and 1991, until the end of the UNTAES period? You don't have to speak about the present day.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: May I answer that now then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the objection, he is -- we have no objection to questions about 1990 and 1991, but then he adds this on about the end of the UNTAES period, which is January of 1997, so again -- I mean, we feel that there's no relevance whatsoever in these issues. If he limits it to 1990, 1991, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well then. 1990 to the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, 1990 to the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No tone.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The town of Vukovar had about 35.000 -- Vukovar had 42.000 inhabitants and there were about 17 and a half thousand Serbs and a large number of Yugoslavs, people who had declared themselves as Yugoslavs. If you look at this percentage-wise, this is 37 percent Serbs and about 17 percent were the Yugoslavs. As far as the town of Vukovar proper is concerned, but according to my information in the Municipality of Vukovar itself, there are about 45 percent of the Serb population and about 15 percent of individuals who had declared themselves as Yugoslavs and many of them too were ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the course -- since you left Vukovar, has that number been reduced in Vukovar and how many? That is since 1992, November, the end of November.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the number dropped drastically. I think that in Vukovar, of that 17 and a half thousand Serbs who lived there, I don't think that there were more than five or six thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did they leave? May we repeat this once again?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They left because of continuous incidents and pressure exerted on them. They were in great fear because before their eyes they saw how Serbian cafes and houses were shelled and blown up and they felt that they were not protected and decided to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, after November 1991, did they all return or did a part of them return?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A portion returned. The other part never returned. It is difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about Slavko Dokmanovic and himself as a man, as a personality, as a character? You got to know him, you worked with him, probably fairly superficially, but can you tell us something of his character? Can he be considered an extreme Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew him, he was a very tolerant man, a very moderate man, and I think they cooperated a fair amount with the Serbs and Croats in Vukovar. And he was elected at the time as president of the municipality, not because he was an extremist Serb nationalist but because he was a moderate man who was able to communicate with people. And as he belonged to the moderate stream, I'm sure that a portion of the Croats voted for him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we say that he was a quiet, calm man, you know, the respect he wielded in the environment in which he lived?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He was a family man, he was a prominent man, he was president of the municipality before these events and during the events, so he was a well-respected man with the population, both the Serb and the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he respected by the extremist Serbs or the moderate Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we can say -- talk about this. We can't say that everybody, all the Serbs, extremists, otherwise there would be no point in talking about this. There were a small number of Serbs that were extremists as there were a small number of Croats that were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he respected by them or was he respected by the majority of moderate Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, the moderate Serbs, the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was respected by the moderate Croats as well, as far as I knew him, because he was a politician and he did cooperate with people well and with the Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that he was accused of killing some 200 peoples in Ovcara, would you believe this?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I would not believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I apologise for taking up five more minutes of your time than I had stipulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor intend to ask many questions? You would prefer now to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that would be probably better, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness that we're going to hear after Mr. Stanimirovic, when the Prosecution completes its cross-examination, the witness has asked for image distortion. We can't do it here, so I should like to ask you for a closed session and then that will be equivalent to the image distortion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there's no objection, there will be a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we probably would not have any objection, but we're not aware of who this witness is. Is it the next witness that is listed? Is it the witness listed as No. 3? Is that correct or ... For the video link conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is an additional witness for which we sought the court's agreement. It is a witness for Mr. Dokmanovic's character, a character witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may have just one moment? Your Honour, I apologise for the brief delay. Cross-examined by Mr. Williamson

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, now, the party that you were affiliated with in 1991 was the Serb Democratic Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this was not the party of democratic change with which Mr. Dokmanovic was associated.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was the Serb Democratic Party advocating autonomy and separatism for Serbs in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party did not have the possibility of becoming registered in Vukovar due to certain obstructions, and the Serbs, via that party, did not take part in Vukovar and the environs at the elections. The protagonist and leader of the SDP, Professor Raskovic, advocated a cultural autonomy of the Serbs, and in the programme itself and the statute of the Serbian Democratic Party, no separation is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the Serb Democratic Party was viewed by Croats as being very radical, much in the same light that Serbs viewed the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think the answer to that is yes, we could say that in that direction because the party later on, when the incidents began to break out, it perhaps deviated from its programme. There was a little more radicalism than was inherent in the programme and as was Professor Raskovic's intention in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, in fact, after Professor Raskovic died, the party changed altogether, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Professor Raskovic died later on, in 1993, and everything had happened until that time. All the events linked to Vukovar and the other parts of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in the meantime, the leadership of the party had been taken over by other persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, in your statement that you provided to the Defence, you indicated that approximately 30.000 persons left Vukovar in 1991 and that most of these were Serbs; is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Of the total number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't hear this part. The speech is interrupted.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think about 30.000 people left Vukovar before the fighting, the battles that took place before Vukovar, mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We heard the last part. Mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can just test it out and see if they're receiving and we are, and if so, then I'll proceed, but if not, then perhaps we need some technical help.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to hear everything that I'm saying there, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the witness, his speech is interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware that a lot of times when we are going through these V-SAT communications to Belgrade and Zagreb, there are temporary interruptions, so this may be a momentary thing when the satellite is out of place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It will take two minutes, I understand, so let us wait here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, I believe when we left off, I'm not sure you were able to hear everything I said and we were unable to get all of your responses, so perhaps I will repeat a little bit of it. Now, you had indicated that approximately 30.000 people left Vukovar prior to the fighting starting, and that the majority of those people were Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I said that in my statement and I now confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, according to the 1991 census, the population of Vukovar was 44.639 persons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I think that there were 42 and a half thousand, but probably the 44.000 figure you mentioned is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And under that same census, it indicated that there were 14.425 Serbs and 4.355 Yugoslavs, so approximately 18 to 19.000 Serbs and Yugoslavs put together.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with that. I have quite different data than the figure you quoted, 37 percent were Serbs and 17 percent were Yugoslavs. Those are the figures, official figures, that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't have these figures in front of me so it's somewhat difficult for me to check that. But you're indicating that 37 percent were Serbs, 17 percent were Yugoslavs, and as I understand your contention --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
