utterances.text: -- that almost all of the Yugoslavs were Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say this. I said that the majority of the Yugoslavs were Serbs because people under certain pressure linked to what was going on, to cover up their nationality, declared themselves Serbs. I did not say everybody but I said the majority and that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, your figure, though, that you say that the majority of people that left were Serbs, even assuming that your figures are correct, which, as I say, don't necessarily agree with the figures that I have given you, but that would be a total of 54 percent of the population, so around 21.000 people. Now, you said that about 30.000 people left, so wouldn't that seem to indicate that a significant number of Croats also left Vukovar during this period?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct. A portion of the Croats left Vukovar in that period. I did not say that that was not correct, I said the majority. But 30.000 were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thirty thousand were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection. You have asked him this for the fifth time, the same thing. The witness never said that 30.000 Serbs left, there were 30.000 people who had left. Of that number, the majority were Serbs. That's what the witness said on several occasions. I don't know why this is relevant, but that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? The reason that I have repeated the question, as I said, because we were interrupted with the break, and I wanted to make sure that all of the witness's statements were put on the record. I'm reading the transcript right here, this was going to be my last question, and then he said, "But 30.000 were Serbs." I'm just trying to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Dr. Stanimirovic, are you saying that 30.000 were Serbs, or that 30.000 people left and that the majority were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In the statement and the minutes, it says that in '91, about 30.000 inhabitants left Vukovar. Of that number, the majority were Serbs. That is clearly stated and in the statement today. I did not say that 30.000 were Serbs on any occasion, at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps that was a mistranslation, but I'm glad that we've cleared that up now. At this time I would like for you to look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 188, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The witness has Exhibit 188 in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Stanimirovic, do you recognise this as being the population statistics for the entire Municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 84.189 of the population census in 1991 existed in Vukovar, yes, that is probably the correct figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, all the way over to the right it indicates a figure of about 6.124 Yugoslavs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, that would be for the entire Municipality of Vukovar. But looking at the figure of 6.000, that would already be less than 17 percent of the entire population of Vukovar city, would it not?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say in percentages. I know the facts and figures that we have even now and that we put forward to the international community regardless of the facts and figures that were written down in 1991 because we had earlier population censuses as well. If you look at the year 1981, you will see that there were 17.000 Yugoslavs at the time, so how come in 1991 that there were 6.000? Were are the other 11.000 Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I think, Doctor, if you look at that, there were also 4.699 in 1971, so might that increase of approximately 12.000 be attributed to this Yugoslav enthusiasm and nostalgia, after the death of Tito?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that we can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at it, if you go all the way over to the left on that and you will see that between 1971 and 1981, there is an increase in the total population of Vukovar municipality, correct, of about 5.000 people, from 76.000 to 81.000?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, at the same time, the number of Croats decreases by about 4.000 people, does it not, from 34.000 to 30.000.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exact. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the number of Serbs decreases from 28.000 to 25.000. So a decrease of about 3.000.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in the same period, the number of Yugoslavs increases by about 12.000. So wouldn't it seem to indicate that both Croats and Serbs declared themselves Yugoslavs during this period since the entire population increased, and that, in fact, perhaps more Croats declared themselves as Yugoslavs than did Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't say because, if you look at these figures, you will see that the number of Croats drops by about four and a half thousand, the number of Serbs drops by about three and a half thousand. That is 8.000 in all. And you can see that the difference between 4.000 and 17.000, 11.000, so we still have 3.000 people lost somewhere in these figures. We can't say that more Croats declared themselves as Yugoslavs, but quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I mean, we can go through the figures for all of the different ethnic groups. I didn't want to actually do that. But I think you will see drops in the numbers of Ruthenes, the numbers of Hungarians, all of the groups reduce in population, and the only one that increases is Yugoslavs, and the total number of people in the municipality increases, so wouldn't this seem to indicate that people from all ethnic groups declared themselves as Yugoslavs in 1981, and then in 1991, as the population of the municipality again continues to grow, the number of Yugoslavs drops but the numbers of all the ethnic groups again go up?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a national division in 1991, so that most probably some of the Croats who previously declared themselves as Yugoslavs in 1981, in 1991 declared themselves as Croats. The question is how much in this Serb euphoria who declared themselves as Yugoslavs were able to say that they were Serbs. This is a dilemma before which we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, the number of Serbs also increased by 6.000 at that time, did it not? So that would again seem to indicate that the Yugoslavs had declared themselves as Serbs again as well, not just Croats? That's my last question on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, why does the Prosecution not bring a democratic (sic) representative? There is a statistics office in Zagreb and in Serbia and they will be able to explain this to us, a demographic representative. I don't where this is leading us. I am raising a question of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might reply to that? Again, Mr. Fila asked this man the question and said, our last person was not qualified to do it but this man is qualified to do it, he's a politician, he knows the statistics. Mr. Fila himself has stood up from the bar table on several occasions and has declared that all Yugoslavs were Serbs. Now, unfortunately we can't cross-examine Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We should be able to cross-examine him when he is putting forward the statistics and the beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On the other hand, you have put quite a few questions on statistical --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Fila never said that all Yugoslavs were Serbs. For example, I declared myself as a Yugoslav and you know full well that I am of Greek origin, so it is not true that all Slavs were Yugoslavs nor that all Yugoslavs declared themselves as Serbs. I never said that. Don't quote me incorrectly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I should say that by and large we regard all these questions as of very little material, almost no material at all to our questions. I mean, we are dealing with some specific facts and the applicable law, not with the statistics, the population increases and decreases and so on. Please, let us move on to other questions that are more relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Stanimirovic, you indicated that you became mayor of Vukovar after the events of November of 1991, at some point in '92 you became President of the Municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. This was at the end of 1993, before the multi-party elections that were held in the republic of Srpska Krajina, after the victory at these multi-party elections where the Radical Party won, then their representatives appointed their President of the Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not clear. When did you serve as President of the Municipality?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Before the multi-party elections that were held at the end of 1993, I was president practically until the beginning of January 1994, a total of three or four months altogether. After the multi-party elections, the Radical Party won a majority in Vukovar, and they appointed their President, Ljubomir Vukicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it was only in the interim period at the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That's right, that's right, exactly, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Caslav Niksic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, he is the individual that was sent by your administration to be the official Serb observer at the Ovcara exhumation in 1996, was he not?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But the Croatian commission did not accept him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that, I'm talking about during the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters can't hear the witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I don't know if we've lost the connection or perhaps I spoke over him. I'm not sure. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, I'm not talking about in the period near the end of UNTAES, I'm talking about during the Ovcara exhumation, he was there and he was present at Ovcara for some period of time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware of an incident on the 11th of September of 1996 in which Mr. Niksic tried to bribe the Jordanian security patrol to gain access to the Ovcara site after the tribunal investigators and forensic experts had left for the day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klein told me that because I cooperated with him, but afterwards, when I talked to Mr. Niksic, he denied this completely and that there was no reason for him to go on his own to Ovcara. He said that he went to get the hub cap of his car or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection once again. It is irrelevant, or should I now ask Mr. Stanimirovic how many Serbs there were at that time when Caslav Niksic was bribing Jordanian soldiers or whatnot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. After consulting my colleagues, I was going to ask the Prosecutor to refrain from asking these questions which are not material to our issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have no questions. Please, could we just have a closed hearing now so that the next witness could be heard behind closed doors and could this witness be marked as DD and I am going to tell you which witness this is or rather show you which witness this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but I should like to thank the witness for testifying. You may now be released. Thank you. So we will move on to our next witness, it will be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. (The Witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand we may now proceed in closed session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The Witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we may now move to the open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: With the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The only problem, Your Honour, is that I don't know who the next witness is. We'll see who turns up. I would like to ask for a witness to be brought tomorrow in the video link, his name is Milos Vojnovic. He's the former President of the Court in Vukovar and we came by him this morning. He would testify instead of Mr. Gradina, who doesn't seem to be there. So if you would allow this witness to take part in the video link tomorrow. He has not been put forward. So far we haven't got the statement. If Mr. Gradina turns up, well and good. If not, we would like to have this other witness who was the President of the Court in Vukovar in 1991. We have some problems in bringing these people, and the witnesses on the video link had some problems, and he told this story to the others and now everybody seems to be afraid to come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? Could Mr. Fila repeat the name of the witness again, and also we would like to have some notice as to the nature of his testimony. If a statement is not available, at least a summary of what he will testify as to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be happy to do so. Vojnovic, Milos, he is the former President of the Court in Vukovar, and he will be testifying as to the circumstances in Vukovar until he was expelled from the court. He will be speaking about his friendship with Mr. Berghofer and the character of Mr. Berghofer, and in that sense, the witness, Mr. Gradina, was proposed, but it seems that he has not turned up. The witness that you now see is Koncarevic, Ilija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Koncarevic, could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me prepare what I need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. ILIJA KONCAREVIC, Sworn: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Koncarevic, did you make a statement which you signed in your own hand to lawyer Mr. Petrovic from my office?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you take a look at that statement and confirm its authenticity, please, the one that you are being shown, the one that is being shown you. You have it in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, then I tender this in evidence as 106 and 106A. Exhibit 106, 106A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Koncarevic, did you graduate from the Faculty of Economics, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Koncarevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was employed in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1990, 1991, that is the period for which we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was already retired at the time. I was retired on the 1st of January, 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you lived as a pensioner?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you one of the founders of the Serbian National Council of the Baranja region?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you its Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did this happen? When was this fact?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of January, 1991, in Sidski Banovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was that organisation? Was it a secret organisation?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a secret organisation. In order to contact with the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you read out the founding act?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are you reading from now?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It is a book published by Ilija Petrovic because I have no other document available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the book's name, title?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is evidence, Prosecution's evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you read it out to us, please, the founding Act, not the declaration, but the statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The founding Act, first of all -- can I begin reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Bearing in mind that the unification of the Slovenes, with the Kingdom of Serbian Montenegro into a uniform state" -- "into a united state."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Into a united state of the Slovenes, the Croats, and Serbs, was brought by the National Council of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes on the 24th of November, 1918, and in view of the fact that when the" --"that the rules of procedure for the National Council of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, all questions related to unification of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs into a national, free and independent state are considered unconditionally a question of the National Council of the three nations whose interests that council will support, confronted by the fact that the Slovenes and Croats have brought separate decisions on seceding from the State of Yugoslavia in which they entered jointly with the Serbs by a decision recognised on the 3rd" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're losing the tone.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Was completely ignored. The Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem does not accept the solutions by which the present Republics of Croatia and Slovenia, without agreement on the part of the Serbian people as Serbia and Western Srem, separate these territories from the territory of the State of Yugoslavia. Second, as the sole legitimate organ of the Serbian, Baranja, Western Srem people in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We already have this document. It's Prosecutor 197, Exhibit 197. Is there any point? It's in English. We've got it in English. Is there any point in reading the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, never mind, Mr. Koncarevic. We have that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you mentioned the 6th of April, 1941, in the declaration?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And why do you mention that particular date?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the date because up until the 6th of April, 1941, when Yugoslavia was attacked, and after that an independent State of Croatia was set up, there was great suffering for the Serbian people and many parts of Croatia changed their ethnic makeup. Many villages and municipalities and whole regions were changed. The structure was changed to the debit of the Serbian people, to the advantage of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us how many Serbian National Councils existed?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were -- first of all, the Serb National Council was set up in July in Silibit (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was the National Council, all-embracing National Council in -- by proclamation, all the Presidents of the Municipalities with a Serb majority became members of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the second Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We set up the second council role because of the specific features of both regions and that it had no territorial links with Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Slavko Dokmanovic, was he a member of the these two Serbian National Councils, first of all of one and then the other?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can say quite responsible that Slavko Dokmanovic was never a member of the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. There seems to be a problem in the translation. A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who entered the Serb National Council and how in Srb in 1990? How were the members elected, slowly.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In Serbia in 1990 -- the Serbian people in its history always took important decisions for its fate on the religious and national gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that is what happened in Srb?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Under the leadership of Professor Raskovic. It was proclaimed that the Serbian National Council that was formed at the time was composed of the Presidents of the Municipalities where there was a Serbian majority in Croatian territory, and the Presidents of the Municipality Boards of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you president of the Great National Council and when was it held? Great National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was President of the Great National Assembly. It was constituted on the 25th of June, 1991, and the first official meeting where the government was proclaimed was also held on the 25th or 26th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us go back to once again. How were the members of the Serbian National Council elected in 1990?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend a meeting, but I was told from the press that the Serbian National Council was proclaimed and that within its composition the Presidents of the Municipalities and whether Serbs had a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they elected by acclamation?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, acclamation. I wasn't there myself, but it was by acclamation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we go back to the Great National Assembly. You were president of the Great National Assembly; it took place on the 25th of June, 1991. When was the government elected?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The government was elected on the 25th or the 26th of September, I don't recall exactly, of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any problems in Beli Manastir? Were there any problems in electing Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Slavko Dokmanovic was at the time the most tragic figure in Croatia. The Serbs did not accept him because of his tolerance towards the Croats when he was the former Mayor -- formerly the Mayor of Vukovar, and the Croats did not want him because he was a Serb, so that he had a great deal of problems. And I know that Goran Hadzic had to intervene on two occasions, and me too once, because we did not have experts for agriculture at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can he then be considered an extremist Serb or a moderate Serb? How did you see him?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We considered him to be a moderate, temperate man, and many Serbs considered him to be a traitor of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you recall a programme shown on Novi Sad television?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in that particular programme, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the attitude adopted by Slavko Dokmanovic was the stand of the Serbian National Council or was it a moderate stand?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He said on the occasion that he was not a member of the Serbian National Council, that he never was a member of the council. And the second thing he said was that he was speaking as the Mayor of Vukovar and the President of both the Serbs and the Croats, and his presentation was completely moderate. It was never coloured in any national colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know the conditions under which this government worked? Well, it was the classical government. You had salaries and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, we did not have salaries. That government had no means at its disposal. There were marketing moves, looking for people on the other side to recognise us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have an army, a policy, a solid territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. This was not under our competencies. We just had people organised in villages, within the villages, and these commanders were proclaimed commanders for the defence of the villages, but we did not have any power or authority over them because the territory was all broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November, 1991, were you in Vukovar and when did you come to Vukovar, when did you reach Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I came from Sid, from the direction of Sid, and I was invited by Hadzic to come to that meeting. I think that I left sometime between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m. and around 1.00, whether a little before or a little afterwards, I found myself in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you come to the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic there and when?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: About what time was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: When he entered, at the beginning of the meeting, which began at about 2.00 p.m., he entered the hall at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many entrances and exits to the hall are there?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did this meeting end, the one at the VELEPROMET building?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Throughout that time, was Slavko Dokmanovic there?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was there inside. He talked about agriculture and also about tilling the land for the winter, about feeding the population, and also the great suffering that would follow, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you last see him that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the end of the meeting, we stood out there and we shook hands and I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was around 3.00 p.m.; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of clothes he wore that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He always wore some kind of hunting uniform of his own, I don't know, a huntsman's uniform. I think it was a huntsman's uniform. It wasn't a JNA uniform, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And one more thing, please. On the 20th of November, were there any civilian authorities on the territory of the City of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Our authority or that of the government does not exist in the area, and in the local communities -- I mean, that is the first time we saw Vukovar. Whether in the local communities they had some kind of authority, I don't really know about that, but I don't think they had it, because then we said that we should establish some kind of authority together with them in order to feed the population, to take care of health, and to take care of children, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can one say that there was military rule at that time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you also get certain permits? Was there freedom of movement or did you have to have a permit?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. There were checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: By the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Approximately when was civilian rule first established in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think that our government, at the beginning of December, passed a decision to establish the Executive Council of Vukovar, and I think that was done sometime by mid-December.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can I conclude that before December this was not possible, and before December in Vukovar there was only military administration?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am stating that with full responsibility, because I was President of the Assembly, after all, and I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic as a person? Did you talk to someone about him?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I would meet Slavko Dokmanovic. And he looks like a humanist to me, rather than a hard-core nationalist or radical or something like that. He was a reasonable man who mainly dealt in agriculture and was preoccupied with agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I could say that he is being accused of having participated in the killing of at least 200 people in October, would you believe that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that he would be capable of spanking his own child, let alone bring arms against a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann? Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think it is your evidence, is it not, that you didn't attend the Serb National Council meeting which took place at Srb near Knin on the 25th of July, 1990; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Slavko Dokmanovic attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it. I read about it in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And therefore you wouldn't have known whether or not he was in fact made a member of the council on that day or at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. Only that much which was said, that the Presidents of Serb Municipalities and Presidents of the Local Committees of the Serbian Democratic Party would become members of this council. This was carried by the press, and I thought therefore that Dokmanovic was included because he was President of a municipality, and that was Vukovar. This was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you attend the government meeting at VELEPROMET on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There was supposed to be an agreement as to how civilian rule would be established on the territory of Vukovar, and this is within the domain of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What capacity did you perform at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: President of the Assembly. To be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you preside over the meeting then as President?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, who did preside over the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to be chaired by Hadzic, but the main speaker was a Colonel, some Colonel whom we found there. I think his surname was Vojnovic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is a colonel in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If he was the main speaker, what did he have to say?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He said that we have nothing to do there for the time being, that we could not establish any kind of government, that there is military rule, military administration there then, and that perhaps it would become possible within a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did the meeting say in response to this?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Attempts were made that we establish this immediately, to set a date for this or something, but it was impossible because the situation was as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, who informed you that the meeting would take place?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Hadzic, by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did he say to you when he informed you that this meeting would occur?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: My first name is Ilija, so he said, "Ilija, come to this meeting. We're going to have a meeting on the 20th of in Vukovar, so come and attend it if you can." That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you attend previous meetings of the government, in particular on the day before this meeting, that's on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, no, no. I attended government meetings perhaps only twice. This was not a real session. There was only -- it was just a meeting. And I also attended another government session after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, how did you get to VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I came with some kind of Combi from Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you drive yourself or did you have someone drive you?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, no. No, no, no. Somebody drove the Combi, and who that was and whose Combi that was, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you on your own or were you with a group of people?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were three or four or five of us there, possibly. I just remember that Josip Pajakovic (phoen) was with me, and the rest -- I think Beretuk (phoen), I think. I don't know his first name. He was doing something in the government. I don't know what post he exactly held. I think he was in the vehicle too. And I can't remember the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at VELEPROMET, did you immediately proceed inside the building?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I stayed for a while in front of the building, because there were some of my acquaintances there, and there were also some people whom I had seen for the first time. So we had brief exchanges of views, we would say "Hello" to each other, and then sometime before 2.00 I walked into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And are you able to recall now some of the people there that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They knew me rather than -- I didn't know them. I knew their faces, but I didn't know their names. I'm very bad at remembering people's names anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you in any sort of military-style uniform on the day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, not me. No. I never wore a uniform throughout the events that are being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any other people there who belonged to the government who were in uniform? I don't necessarily mean JNA uniform but I mean military-style uniform.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, we had different uniforms because our hygienic conditions, you know, and everything were such -- the easiest thing was to wear an olive green-grey uniform and camouflage and to wear that, so, yes, yes, some people did wear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, this Colonel, I think you said he was a JNA Colonel, was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any other military people present apart from the Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the Colonel, when I walked into the room, there was not a single other military man in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him there that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know him personally. No, I walked in before Arkan arrived, but I only heard that he had arrived but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone -- I withdraw that. Did people come and leave the meeting from time to time during the course of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Only Hadzic went out of the meeting because there was an enormous number of journalists from all over the world outside, so he was asked to come out but no one else came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when Hadzic went out, he gave a press conference, did he?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about what to do with Croatian prisoners at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, this was not within our competence. That was the first time I saw Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this something that you're saying absolutely didn't happen or is it just something that you say you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not the previous question -- could you repeat your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Can you hear me now clearly?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you said -- you said that there was no discussion about what to do with Croatian prisoners. My next question was --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, because it was not within our competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic told us loud and clear that those people and that all other authorities and powers were under the military in Vukovar, so it would have been pointless to discuss that. Perhaps someone tried to but it didn't mean a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is, is this something that you know categorically and absolutely did not occur, or are you simply saying that you didn't know of it?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what happened. I don't understand the question, whether this had happened or had not happened. What event are we talking about? What is this "happening"?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the answer has been provided by the witness. Look at the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I don't agree with you, Mr. Fila. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry, I heard him answer in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is this: When you say that there was no discussion about what to do with Croatian prisoners at that meeting, my question is: Is that something that you say absolutely did not happen or is it something that you yourself didn't hear or didn't know about?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Please. This was a meeting without any minutes and without a set agenda. If someone mentioned something like that in front of this Colonel, I allow that that is possible, but I didn't take part in that and this was not an item on the agenda. And it was not within the domain of our competencies at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that you had an agenda for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have an agenda for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, what did you mean when you said "This was not an item for the agenda"? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I mean there was no agenda. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, how well do you know Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not that well except that I met him during the mentioned events.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many times would you have met him in total?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting of the assembly and preparing the work of the assembly, this Ministry that he was in charge of, where he really had a tough time, he came and he asked me to help him with my influence or to see whether I had some connections, whether I could do something to help, et cetera, so there were quite a few contacts. But they certainly were not that frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How frequently had you met him, known him, and spoken to him prior to the government being elected in, I think September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you hadn't known him before that time; is that correct? You hadn't known him personally. You may have known of him --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Before those events, I did not know Slavko Dokmanovic, I only read about him in the press as the Mayor of Vukovar when he was elected, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I take it you didn't know anything about his family.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Once I met his family as I went through his village. I met his wife, but I didn't meet his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that before or after this meeting on the 20th of November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That was way back in the spring of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What time did you leave VELEPROMET on that day of the meeting of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Around 3.00, sometime after 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what route did you follow in order -- when you left?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I went on the same road that I came in on, via Negoslavci to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the trip going home, the return journey? What were the traffic conditions like?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't notice anything special except that it was different than the conditions on which I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In what sense was it different?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I took the same Combi back to Sid, the same one that I took from Sid to there. I didn't know this man and I don't know who drove it and I don't know whose Combi it is, and then I went back to Sid and I took my own car back to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On your way back to Sid, did you see Mr. Dokmanovic at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any particular types of vehicles on the roads that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I sat in the vehicle and I was talking en route, perhaps there was something on the road, but I didn't see anything. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did you stop at any stage on the way between VELEPROMET and Sid?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? No questions. Mr. Koncarevic, I have a couple of questions for you. You may be of some assistance to us by clarifying one or two points. First of all, at that particular meeting of the government on the 20th of November, were problems, the various problems arising out of the destruction of Vukovar discussed?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You know, seven years have gone by, and to remember everything correctly and to say with full responsibility who said what, that would really be pretentious for my age, you know, I really couldn't -- we were shocked, you know, with the situation and everything we found there, and we talked about that and we looked at one another. We didn't even have any minutes. So it was a meeting that referred to the future more than saying what should be done when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say that this particular meeting was a sort of emergency meeting since the government had already met the previous day, on the 19th of November, in Erdut, and if so, how would you explain --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think that the point of the meeting was -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Did I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think that Hadzic convened the meeting so that the government could impose itself as some kind of an authority for the town in the future. I don't think he had anything specific in mind, what he could do right now, but I think that Mr. Hadzic could say more about that than I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think, if I'm not wrong, on the previous day the government had decided -- actually had issued a sort of decree, a decision, whereby the JNA should be under the control of the government. Now, in light of that, how was the suggestion by the Colonel of the JNA -- how did people react to the suggestion by the Colonel -- could you wait one moment, please? -- how did people at that meeting react to the suggestion by the Colonel of the JNA that the military rule should prevail?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They reconciled themselves to it. That's the way it was. We didn't have anything and they had everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: A final question: We were given by the Defence the agenda and a summary of the minutes, I think -- again, if I'm not wrong -- of the government's meeting on the 19th of November. How would you explain that there was no agenda -- there were no minutes for the meeting of the 20th of November? As I say, the day before minutes and an agenda and minutes of the meeting were carefully drawn up.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? If that was the case on the 19th -- I'm not a member of the government and I cannot answer why things were the way they were and how things were, et cetera, and as far as the 20th is concerned, perhaps that is something to do with the message that Hadzic sent me. He said, "Come if you can."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there is no objection to the witness being released. Thank you, Mr. Koncarevic, for testifying. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps I should explain something, Your Honour? Half of the witnesses are coming from Vukovar and half from Novi Sad, not a single witness is from Belgrade, so I really have no idea when who arrives. I am a bit embarrassed by all this but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Fila, it is not your fault. You should not be embarrassed. But I hope the registrar is going to have the next witness as soon as possible. I may probably turn to the Prosecutor and ask whether they have been able to prepare the famous stills.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an ongoing saga. We have tried, at the end of last week, on several occasions to get the photos done. The paper that was necessary for this had not been received, and I understood that it was held up in procurement. We were told that they would have these in the video unit today and Mr. Dzuro from our office went down to make it and was advised they still had not received the paper for printing the photographs. I spoke with Ms. Featherstone at the lunch break and made her aware of this and she said she would follow up with Mr. Falces and try to get this sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next witness is Goran Hadzic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, could you please kindly stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: GORAN HADZIC Examined by Mr. Fila

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, did you make a statement to the investigator in my office that we're going to show you and is that your signature on the statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender this in evidence. It will be number D107 and D107A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, where did you go to school, what university did you graduate from, what schools have you, and when?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Borovo Naselje Vukovar gymnasium, that is secondary school in Vinkovci, and I studied economics in Osijek, but I never graduated. After the second year, I left university and went to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the first multi-party elections, were you elected as a member of the municipal assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected on behalf of the SDP, as it was called, the Party of Democratic Change.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He comes from a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he elected at that same list for a member of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were you on the SDP list, the Party of Democratic Change?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: After the system that reigned in Yugoslavia, we set up a party of a Yugoslav orientation with Serbs and Croats both taking part and we wanted Yugoslavia to remain. We did not want to form nationalist parties, and that is why I was in the SDP party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There was a Serb party registered and put up for elections in Vukovar that year, was there?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not in Vukovar. There was the Serb Democratic Party in Knin, but we Serbs did not want to have a nationalist party to come forward with a nationalist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you choose the SDP then?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Because the belief that prevailed with the Serb people, that the Croats were in favour of the Yugoslavia and that they wanted to see it survive. Especially the people such as my father and people like -- like-minded people. We were not able, nor did we want to, make parties with -- of Serb orientation before the elections. Had we done so before the elections, I could never have explained to my father or like-minded people that we were not to blame for the victory of the HDZ in Croatia. This way we accepted the Croatian party but, in addition to this, Croatia opted for the nationalist option and seceding from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How was Slavko Dokmanovic elected as President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko was elected as member in the Municipal Assembly at a meeting, democratically by secret ballot, there were two candidates as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the Croats vote for him as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A considerable portion of Croats voted for him. They were not nationalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he a moderate or an extremist Serb at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was taken to be a very moderate Serb, and some extremist Serbs hated him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Later on, were you President of the Prime Minister of the government in the region? How was the government set up? How were you elected?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The government was set up after Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia, that is to say, after the unilateral decision on the part of Croatia to secede because it was not recognised by the world at the time. We set up a government, we convened a meeting of all the deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar and all the other Municipal Assemblies from the area of Slavonia and Baranja and all the other deputies from Slavonia and Baranja, as I say, and they were Serbs for the most part but there were other nationalities as well, Hungarians, I'm not sure whether there were any Croats but I think there were. And they gave me a mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you set up a government, you proposed the government at this Great National Assembly. How did Slavko Dokmanovic come to be Minister of Agriculture?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was a very honourable man, and as you know, he was and is -- he had graduated from the faculty of farming and he was nearby and I was able to appoint him. I appointed him as such and politically, this also corresponded to us because he was very hard-working.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he easily elected or were there those Serbs who did not want to elect him?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: With all the reasonable Serbs, this was okay, but there were not a lot of them. Most extremists attacked him, and I had a lot of problems and had to use all my authority to have Slavko appointed Minister. I thought that he was very valuable to me and I see that I had not made a mistake because he was the only man that was able to undertake this matter and all the peace agreements that we adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did the extremist Serbs criticise him for?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: He was criticised because -- and I don't think Slavko was to blame there -- but they said that he had given over Vukovar to the Croats. These are criticisms that are untenable. He was for the Yugoslav option. And while we were forming the SDS, Slavko was in contact with Zagreb and he brought executive secretaries of the SDP to Trpinja. Those were the basic accusations made against Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The role of your government, what conditions did you have for functioning? Did you have a salary, police, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We had nothing of a normal government. We had no salaries, we couldn't have an army or a police force for practical reasons because we were a Serb region within Yugoslavia, and all this existed on the territory of former Yugoslavia. We formed a government under very difficult conditions. The territory was divided up in half, and for the most part, we did not have any contacts with the other part of the territory for a considerable time. We had to go -- pass a lot of kilometres to set up links, telephones did not work, there was no electricity, no water. It was very difficult to work under such conditions. But we tried to perform a political function, we tried to work with the people, to have the people stay on the territory, and for life to carry on as normally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you undertake anything to change this marginal role on the part of the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did. We adopted several decisions, we wrote letters, but this did not have much effect, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you hold a meeting of your government on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Let me recall the date. In Erdut, yes, it was the meeting on the 19th of November in Erdut, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to show you the minutes from that meeting. It is Defence Exhibit D53. Would you take a look at it, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the minutes from the meeting and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the conclusion under point 5. Could you read it and tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The government of the Serbian (translation unclear) should have units on its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did that mean? Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We had practical problems with the functioning of the government because there was still the conditions of war. The territory, as I said a moment ago, was cut into half, was divided, and each village had its points, army points, and you had to have a permit to move through these check points so that a Minister, for example, was not able to perform his functions. He had to have five permits issued in order to pass through the region, and we wanted this to be recognised and we wanted to do something with regard to this civilian section, and we tried to bring in a decision which nobody accepted. We just brought in that particular decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you read once again what item 5 states?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "The government of the Serb region should be above the units of the JNA on its territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the future tense?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a function -- it is the day before we went to Vukovar, so we were planning to ask them to grant this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that particular moment you had no competences (sic) over the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I thought that was quite clear but I don't seem to have explained it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: From the fact that we were seeking this, asking for this, it is quite evident that this was not the situation. Had we had that, we would not have had to ask for it, and if we had had good will to realise this, this could not have been done in one day, so we needed at least ten to 15 days to implement this, and we needed, in fact, 15 days to one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was convened for the following day, for the 20th of November, according to those minutes?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We had a lot of problems with Vukovar, problems not only with the Croats but also with the Serbs who were on the other side and who did not respect and recognise the government, and we knew that Vukovar was liberated and that we would have to go there. As President, I did not have not the courage but the political wisdom to convene a government meeting there because the question was that we did not -- and Ministers who were intellectuals, part of them were afraid to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who were they afraid of? Who were they afraid of; could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were afraid of threats from the Serbs who said that they did not recognise our government, and there were individual threats as well, not towards myself but threats were made against Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, and he was very brave to go there. I convened a meeting and I said, anybody who can come, please, to come. If not, then that was another matter. Some of the Ministers could not reach the meeting place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there minutes taken, records? Did you have an agenda?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. I tried to see the Ministers who had arrived, but there were no conditions for the regular work and functioning of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that meeting was held and how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The meeting, I can tell you this precisely, was held in the VELEPROMET premises in Vukovar. As far as the time is concerned, as far as I recall, I arrived there somewhere before 2.00 p.m., perhaps 1.30 p.m., and the government meeting began somewhere around 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've lost the time it lasted.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The meeting lasted one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you leave the hall during that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I left the hall once or twice. I gave a statement to some foreign television network. I did not preside over the meeting, chair the meeting, although I had intended to chair it, but I had to leave the rostrum, leave the table, and sit down as an ordinary member with the other members in the audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we now see a tape, the D2 tape, from the VELEPROMET meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was around 1.50, 52 or 53 minutes, 1.52, 1.53.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Two or three minutes. We can start the tape rolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you see the tape, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, we can't at the moment. Your Honour -- here we are. May we take it back to -- let's start it again, please. Rewind it to 13.55, for example. May we rewind it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, when you see yourself there, please tell us to stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Stop. Yes. I can see myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would the usher show the photographs, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you recognise yourself on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't think we need see the tape any further now. Thank you -- well, let's see it for another few seconds. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is more important is how long did the meeting last and can you tell us at the government meeting what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The meeting, as far as I recall, lasted for about one hour, about until 3.00 p.m. We discussed -- it was not -- it was a meeting, an informal talk, discussion, about the future of the civilian population that had remained in Vukovar. About food supplies, bread supplies, more or less social matters. It was not easy to bring in a conclusion because the meeting was chaired by a Lieutenant Colonel, he did not have any special competences, although he was introduced as the commander of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was the -- was the town administered by military rule or civilian rule?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, military rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you introduce civilian rule, civilian administration?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We tried seven days later to do this, but I think that after the new year, this happened after the new year, perhaps even a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you leave VELEPROMET on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think I left after the meeting, somewhere around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was that the last time you saw Slavko Dokmanovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since when have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have known Slavko since before the war, almost 25 years, all in all. I've known him for almost 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of man is he? What is the general opinion of him as a man?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the general opinion is that Slavko as a man is an intelligent man, that he is a professional in his job, that above all, that he is tolerant and reasonable and that he had a lot of sympathies with the local inhabitants, and it is not immodest to say that both the Serbs, the Croats, and other nationalities always had sympathies for him. He was always a reasonable option and never an extreme nationalist option.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Serb National Council for (translation unclear)?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic, as is common knowledge, was elected to the -- in Srb in July, somewhere in July 1990, and after the decision of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, the first meeting that was held afterwards, he left the council and, although he was co-opted into the council because he was put forward by the Knin leadership, the leadership in Knin, and as the representatives of the Serbs, Slavko went there. But as I talked to him about that problem, he told me that at similar meetings he would also be a representative of the Croats in the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you say that he left the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he left the Serb National Council at the -- of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar before my very eyes. I was present on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he in the second Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not, and he did not even know of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you read the book -- have you read the book by Ilija Petrovic about the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have got the book, and when I saw the way in which Ilija Petrovic wrote the book, I just looked through it and threw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know why he called him an incapable President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to Ilija Petrovic and some other Serb nationalists --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you thought that they thought he was incapable because he was not a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to Ilija Petrovic, but I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What don't you agree with?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That Slavko was incapable. He was a very capable man, but he was not a nationalist, and I do not agree that he was incapable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While in VELEPROMET, on the photograph, there was somebody standing next to you in the photograph. Who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You can see Zeljko Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you wearing the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the uniforms are similar but not the same, not identical. I bought mine in Novi Sad. I don't know where he came by his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were those uniforms uniforms of your government?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. I just wore the uniform for practical reasons because there was no electricity and no water, and I had to wear something. I should have worn a suit, which was not physically possible in the war conditions that prevailed. So to blend in with the environment and the atmosphere, everybody wore some kind of uniform, and that's why I wore that particular uniform. It was a nice one. There were not many of them. There were in 1992, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are they uniforms of the regular JNA army?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just bought the uniform, I think in an American shop in Novi Sad, or a private firm, a private shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, was Slavko Dokmanovic wearing a uniform like that at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not have a uniform like me. He had a mixed-coloured one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When leaving VELEPROMET at the end of the meeting of the government, did you give any interviews?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave an interview in the VELEPROMET compound and I gave an interview later on, perhaps somewhere around 4.00 or 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., I don't recall whether it was dark or -- it was at the end of the day, at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you say? Where did you come from? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Belgrade television asked me what had happened, what I was doing. I said that I had come from Vukovar, and that as the government had a very poor influence at that time, I said that we had held a government meeting of sorts for the people to see that the government was not afraid to go to Vukovar, and I had to say this because many people didn't believe that we would be going there, and that's what I said, that we bore in mind the fact that attention was paid to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you mention any war prisoners, courts, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As we were part of Yugoslavia and regardless of the fact that we were not recognised, we did have courts of the first and second degree -- you probably know that -- and I said that we strove to see that justice was done and that no mistakes were made, that the people were justly tried and either sentenced or released.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you said that it was better to have 100 people than have somebody who was innocent -- guilty?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I said that it would be better to leave 100 criminals go rather than have one person innocent condemned. And I think that today. That is what I strove for throughout my work in politics and I'm sure that the Croatian side is well aware of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you spoke of courts, did you have in mind the regular courts that existed at that time or some sort of popular national courts?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I had in mind the courts already in existence, the municipal and community courts, county courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before you left Vukovar with regard to the negotiations in Erdut and the Erdut agreement, did Slavko Dokmanovic play a role?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic, as I said in my introductory part, helped me in -- with Vance's plan.
