He played one of the key roles together with me and some other people in seeing that the Dayton agreement was a success and that an agreement was signed. Had Erdut not have been signed, Dayton would not have been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he played a key role -- Would you please repeat the role over the Erdut agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost the tone again. We did last time.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As far as Slavko himself took part, there were three key individuals, three or four key individuals, and Slavko was one of them. He took part, and half his authority was used there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he replaced in his duties as President?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had problems because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about 1995, the Erdut agreement, and I'm not sure how that is relevant to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is highly relevant. Let me explain. Not for your Prosecution but it is highly relevant for the character of the individual that you are trying here. That is what I had in mind. So only in that sense, Mr. Williamson, is it relevant, nothing else. He was a man of peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, the signing of this agreement, did he perform the role of a man of peace in favour of the peaceful reintegration of the area into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there was a great deal of impact and Slavko played a great role as a man of peace, and somebody wanted -- people wanted to liquidate him and even at that price he played the role of a man of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I have summarised correctly, when you gave your interview in Sid and the other interviews, you tried to assert the government which, in fact, was not of any great importance.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood correctly. The government of Slavonia and Baranja did not have any great importance later on either because the Srpska Krajina region was set up and the government was marginal. Slavko Dokmanovic was not elected to the government of Srpska Krajina. No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Some mention was made of the fact that you gave up on your candidacy to run as the President for the next term. Did you give up on it yourself or did you lose elections?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I lost the election. I was the candidate of the Serb Democratic Party in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you didn't give up?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't give up and I had never thought of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, one further question: You knew Slavko Dokmanovic, you said. Do you know that something happened in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: At the time of these events that we're speaking of, we didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: And later we heard from Croatian television and press that something very terrible had happened at Ovcara, according to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear part of the statement made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Also some of the people we knew -- we asked them whether they knew something about this and no one said that they knew anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I were to tell you now that Slavko Dokmanovic is being accused of having been at Ovcara during that period of time while you had this government meeting and that he took part in the killing of all these people, having known Slavko Dokmanovic, would you believe all of this?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am 100 percent sure that that is not correct, and no one who knows Slavko Dokmanovic could believe a thing like that. I can even mention to the court that I heard rumours that some idiots and fools, I don't know how to call these people, who did this, said that they would -- now Slavko is being accused of Ovcara, and had they been there, they would have killed him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to take a 20-minute break, and after that, there will be cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson? Cross-examined by Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, on the 20th of November of 1991, what time did you arrive at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I said that I arrived sometime after 1.00 p.m., probably around 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And where were you before that time on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was the route that you took from Erdut to VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really think about it, but I think I came via Borovo Naselje to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you go through Dalj and Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It is only logical, Erdut, Dalj, Borovo Selo, Borovo Naselje, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty making it through that route on that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were some problems. You couldn't really get by. It was quite a terrible site. But there weren't any obstacles on the road, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you didn't encounter any fighting on the way between Erdut and VELEPROMET, I take it?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see any direct fighting, although in Vukovar I heard sporadic gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Vukovar, did you go directly to VELEPROMET or did you drive around the city at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: First we came to VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how had you informed the people that they were to be at this meeting? Was it at the meeting the prior day in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what about people like Ilija Koncarevic who were not present at the meeting in Erdut; how did you make him aware of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I only called Ilija on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And where did you call him from?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I called him from Novi Sad or Erdut because there was only one telephone in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did you tell the ministers the purpose of this meeting was to be?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The main purpose was to show up in Vukovar and to see that they were not -- that we were not afraid, so that they would see that we were not afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And as I understand it, this was the first meeting that your government had held in Vukovar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It was not a session of the government, it was just a meeting. It was the first time that the government people came to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And if you can, just once again tell us what was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were discussions without an agenda on a wider subject matter about supplies for the city and all these problems that the civilian rule authorities should deal with. This Lieutenant Colonel from the army also spoke about prisoners of war who were there, but we did not have any jurisdiction over them. I personally was afraid and I advocated a fair trial for the prisoners so that nothing bad would happen to them, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there was then some discussion at this meeting about what was going to happen to prisoners; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not what I'm saying. This was just mentioned. But we were not competent to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, after the meeting concluded, how long did you remain at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I remained at VELEPROMET very briefly, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: After that, after this interview I gave in Sid, I probably went to Novi Sad to see my family because that's where my wife and my children were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it's my understanding that you went directly from VELEPROMET to Sid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not 100 percent correct because I took a drive in the car through the centre of Vukovar. I didn't manage to go out anywhere because everything had been mined. We only stopped in the centre and then we went back and headed towards Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when the fighting was going on in Eastern Slavonia in the autumn of 1991, did you have any type of military role?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No military role. Neither I personally nor my government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you explain again why you would wear a uniform then during this period? What was the reasoning for that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can repeat what I said, and that is that the first reason was that practically all people wore uniforms, so people who wore civilian clothes were actually different. And since I was Prime Minister of this government, it would not have been decent for me to be in a dirty shirt and in a crumpled suit, and there were no possibilities of getting a clean shirt every day and having your suit ironed, so that was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this was just done because you couldn't wash clothes?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: And also, the other reason, because other people wore uniforms and had we worn civilian clothes, we would have been different from the other inhabitants in the area, so we would have caused additional revolt because there was already some revolt toward certain presidents, ministers, et cetera, as we can assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you say that although your uniform was similar to the one that Arkan was wearing, but it was not identical; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: On this recording, I cannot see whether it was identical, and I don't think it's really important. I bought myself this uniform, and whether someone else bought the same uniform before or after that, I don't know, but now I can't even remember what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the uniform, you and Arkan also seemed to be wearing very similar berets with Serb flags on them. Is there any connection there, or was this once again just another coincidence?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We couldn't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear the rest of the answer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The sign was the same. This was a Serb tri-coloured flag, that is the Serb sign, as far as I can see in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was your affiliation with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. No special affiliation. He came to fight and, well, it was said of him that he was brave, and I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, isn't it a fact that he had accompanied you from Erdut on that day, driving to VELEPROMET, because you expected some difficulties in getting through to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We needed that. It's not that we had to penetrate through the area, but we didn't want any incidents to occur in Vukovar because Arkan had sufficient authority in order to prevent this kind of incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So did he also travel with you when you left VELEPROMET after the meeting to Sid?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You don't recall who went with you from VELEPROMET to Sid?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In the car, it was only the driver and myself, and I don't know who else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So did you see Arkan again later that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that he was in Sid too, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you in any way associated with his paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, not in any way was I associated with his unit. I didn't know that he had a paramilitary unit. In Serbia they could have been paramilitaries, but here he was a volunteer, and I don't know what kind of units he had, military or paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, was he part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Everyone there who was fighting against Croatia which tried to secede from Yugoslavia and which attacked the JNA was, in a way, part of the JNA. Everyone who was fighting was part of the JNA, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that would include Seselj's forces and Bokan's and all of these other paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: During my time there, I didn't meet any of them out there, Seselj, Bokan, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As president of Serb district, did you have control over elements of the Serb forces that were fighting in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, not over anyone. Only the military component.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, did you have any influence over the Territorial Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We did not have direct influence over the Territorial Defence, although we tried to organise these village units which were on our territory. I say "our territory," if you understand what I mean, that the district was divided into two parts, so these were these Serb villages, Trpinja, Borovo Selo, Dalj, et cetera. They had some village guards at the beginning of the conflict, but later, when the JNA came, all of this was within the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know Stanko Vojonovic (phoen) and Miroljub Vujovic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And these men were Territorial Defence unit commanders, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I heard that only after the war. I did not know them in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you had no contact with them when the fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I met Stanko only in 1992 or 1993 in a cafe and Miroljub in 1992 when he was some kind of an official in the National Defence in the Vukovar Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you're saying you met Miroljub Vujovic only in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his name and surname in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, isn't it a fact that just a week after the events at Ovcara, on the 28th of November, your government appointed Miroljub Vujovic to the Executive Council responsible for running the City of Vukovar and that this was an order signed by you?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. It may be so, but I didn't know him then. This proposal was made to me by the President of the Municipality of Vukovar, and I accepted that because I didn't know everyone else personally either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And who was it that had made this proposal?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: If that's what you say so, but I don't remember now that Miroljub was there, but I believe you, that he was there, Srbobran Bibic, who was President of the Executive Council of the Municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, in the days after the 20th of November, there was a lot of talk in Vukovar about what had happened at Ovcara, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was not in Vukovar, and I didn't hear such stories in Vukovar. I heard stories about Ovcara, as I told the Defence attorney, my previous conversation through the Croatian media, but nobody corroborated it to me then. I even went to Sremska Mitrovica, to the prison there, to see the prisoners, and I was pleased to have seen people who were alive there. So I thought that the stories about Ovcara were lies because the Croatian media spoke of several thousand victims at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I mean certainly in your position as President of the Serb District, you would have heard something about the mass execution of 200 or more men on territory under your control? No?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, probably I should have heard about it, but, regrettably, I did not hear about it. It would have been a good thing had I heard about it beforehand because I could have prevented it from happening, and had I heard about it afterwards, I would have made an effort to have these people arrested and held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to put it to you that you did know in advance what was going to happen to these people, and that, in fact, their fate was decided at this government meeting at VELEPROMET on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are alleging something that is quite wrong. I am here under oath, and I swear that we didn't know what would happen at Ovcara and what did happen at Ovcara, and I swear not only to you, but I swear before God.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So these men were not held at the JNA barracks for a couple of hours while your government deliberated their fate at VELEPROMET? That is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am telling you that. I did not know that they were at the barracks. I heard that there were prisoners in VELEPROMET who were later taken to Mitrovica, and all of these events that you are talking about, the hospital, Vukovar, I heard about that now, after all of these events, only a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you gave an interview in Sid on the evening of the 20th of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this time --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That is true, yes, I gave an interview, and you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that that be shown, and I have transcripts, please, which I can provide to the court and to the Defence. And if this can be shown, please? I would ask that the clip of the video be shown at this time, please. Your Honour, I understand it will be just a moment. (Videotape played) (Interpreter's translation of interview between Nino Brajovic and Goran Hadzic) NB: Here we are in Sid, on the road to Vukovar. The Prime Minister of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, Goran Hadzic, has just arrived from Vukovar. We have been informed that you held a meeting of the government in Vukovar. What were the main resolutions? GH: This was the first meeting of the government in the future capital of our Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. In addition, to the resolutions and the normalisation of life and the restoration to some kind of normalcy, our main resolution was that the disdained Ustashas, whom we have captured, would not leave the territory of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, that they cannot be transported to Serbia, because Serbia is not at war and that the army which helped us capture them ... they are not soldiers. They are paramilitary formations and they can be tried only by these people here, that is, the people of our Serb District which has been recognised, and which has its own judiciary. We have also a second instance court, and we could possibly have a third instance court at the federation level of the second Yugoslavia. We also have our district and municipal courts. We have agreed with the military authorities to have these Ustashas detained in our detention camps, here in the surroundings of Vukovar. Since one group of Ustashas has already been taken to Sremska Mitrovica, I have personally taken the responsibility to bring these people - if that is the right term to use for them at all, "people" - to bring them back and put those who are guilty on trial. Those who are not guilty will, of course, be released and we will let them rebuild our town with us. NB: According to your estimate, how many members of the Croatian paramilitary formations are there? Our data vary. Two hundred people surrendered two days ago. Today, about one thousand surrendered at the Borovo agricultural farm. What is the exact figure? GH: I think the figure is somewhere around three thousand Ustashas in uniforms, although there is a large number of them hiding among the civilians. There are also a lot of good people. Our main task is to investigate this and prevent the innocent from being punished or persecuted. It is better to have a guilty person get away with it than to punish an innocent person. This is our task and now that we have the law, the police, and other organisations, we will do our utmost to prevent the persecution of ... NB: Could you tell us in brief something about the implementation of the civilian authorities in Vukovar? GH: We have made our first step today. We prepared for this event. Unfortunately, I was too big an optimist. I did not think Vukovar was so badly destroyed. When I saw it today ... this is, really, it cannot be described with words, but there is literally no house that is left undamaged. There are even corpses lying on the streets. We should first have the Ministry of Health, that is Agriculture, that is veterinarians and doctors do something to prevent the infection from spreading. They should do something to remove the bodies from the streets. Then the normalisation should follow, as we planned. Today I have spoken to the people who have borne the brunt of the war. They are the inhabitants of Petrova Gora settlement, without whom our battle for Vukovar would be lost. I would like to take this opportunity to thank them for everything they did and to establish organs that will agree with representatives of these people to set up civilian authorities in the town ... It has been agreed that there will be no military authorities in Vukovar, maybe only for a few days, but the plan is to introduce civilian authorities maybe only for a few days. NB: Does that mean that you will soon take off your uniform? GH: Well, I am a man, a representative of the Serb people, and if the Serb people who have chosen me think that we should not further expand the borders we have established, I will take my uniform off. I personally think I should remain in uniform for some time because the Serb borders are much farther away than where they are at the moment. NB: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We can stop the tape at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, what do you mean when you say "our main resolution was that the detained Ustashas would not leave the territory of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I said this only for the purposes of political marketing and in order to promote the government which did not have support among the people, and, if you noticed, my conclusion in the latter part was to ease tensions and to have some kind of normalisation and to let people go, and I tried to prevent a possible euphoria among the people and I called upon all to act with reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it's easing tensions by saying that you felt like you should expand your borders further?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as the borders of the Serb lands are concerned and my opinion how far the Serb state should go, I don't think that this is the right place to discuss that. If you think it is, we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you a question. You have indicated that you were trying to ease tensions. Do you think that it in any way eased tensions by having a pronouncement from the president of the Serb district that you felt like the Serb border should be expanded further, obviously at the expense of the Croats? How did this ease tensions?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. To whose detriment it would be if somebody took your house? Would it be to your detriment or to the detriment of the person who took your house away from you? I was talking about the territory that belonged to the Serb people and then this went to the detriment of the Serb people. You don't really need a lot of -- you don't really need to look into the future very much; you can see now what the situation is like in the Serb district. And as I was speaking about this, as I spoke about tension, I was speaking about prisoners, I wasn't talking about borders. Borders have nothing to do with these tensions. The Americans killed about ten people in Texas when they wanted to change borders. And this is Serb land; it was never Croatia. However, unfortunately, the world decided differently, and I don't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, if this was just an effort on your part to enhance the position of your government, why was it necessary to go into all this detail about prisoners? Wouldn't it have been enough just to say, "We had a meeting, we have made resolutions to establish normal life in Vukovar," and then to go on to say that, "We've established ourselves as the government"? Why go into all this detail about prisoners? What was the reasoning for that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: What is normal now and what seems normal to people now was not normal then, and I had to say something so that, as the saying in our country goes, "The wolf would not be hungry and that all the sheep would remain intact too."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about your statement that you said you had taken personal responsibility to bring people back from Sremska Mitrovica? This was also for public consumption?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Let me say this. We never asked for this and we never could have gotten it. They had adequate accommodation there, as adequate as can be in prison, and most of them or, rather, all of them were released, according to the decision made by then Prime Minister Milan Panic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, we know that, in fact, that some of the "detained Ustashas," as you refer to them, did not leave the territory, the Serb district; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We know that now, but then as far as the Ustashe are concerned, I have to explain something to you. Perhaps you are not familiar with this. The Serb and the Croatian sides -- rather -- used very offensive vocabulary about one another. The Croats called us Chetniks, slaughterers, and we call them Ustashas and fascists. And at a round of negotiations with the Croatian delegation, when I was president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, I agreed I think with Mr. Hoda Sardonic (phoen), I think it was him, that we get rid of that kind of vocabulary and that we talk normally. But this was at the end of 1991, and there was a lot of tension on both sides, among the people, and it was normal vocabulary then, although I can see now that it was not normal vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the fact that these decisions and these meetings and these interviews are now being brought out into public and into the light of day has nothing to do with you saying that this was just for public consumption at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question, but if I have understood you correctly, what I said, regardless of the government decision, I was only able on the -- answer to the government why I said something that was not agreed upon. I thought this to be a political move, and I made my own decisions and did not suffer any consequences afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, you had said that you needed to do this to satisfy the people. Was there pressure on your government from the people to do something about Croatian criminals, Croatian war criminals?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: If you followed my statement, and I'm sure you did, then you were able to see that I was very sceptical with regard to the number of Croatian criminals and that I said finally that the criminals should be punished, but the vast majority of the people were not criminals. It was difficult to say to the Serbs that it was not the -- not all the Croats were to blame, although a significant portion were, because in that case, I could have been killed by a bullet fired from the Serb side. So something had to be said to pacify the people, pacify the people and prevent evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, when you say that those who were guilty would be put on trial, guilty of what?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: For the killing of the Serbs. I don't know whether you know that a lot of Serbs died at the very beginning when Croatia attacked the Serbs, when it attacked the military barracks, army barracks, and when it set fire to Serb enterprises, newspapers, and so on and so forth. Serb houses were fired at, prominent Serbs were killed and thrown into the river. So I advocated what you advocate today, and I hope that you will be just in your advocation (sic) of that, that is, to bring criminals to trial, and you can only determine who is guilty at a court, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: There were a lot of Croats killed as well in Vukovar during the course of this battle, and certainly on the 20th of November. What efforts did you make, or your government make, to put anyone on trial for those crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, we did not know about these crimes at a time when something could be done about it. As the President of the Serb Krajina -- Srpska Krajina region, I wanted to determine the truth, and I signed a decision, apart from the decision of the Knin government, which prohibited exhumation. I allowed this to take place, as President for, exhumation to start. I don't know why it was not started. And when I was President of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in 1996, and I shall do everything in my power to bring the culprits to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we spoke about the President. Could he please say when he is thinking about the function of President, because there was the government where Slavko Dokmanovic was a Minister and then you have the other government where Mr. Dokmanovic was not president. So when you ask about the function of President, would you make it clear what you are thinking of? This is no objection; it's just in the interests of detail and precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I follow exactly what Mr. Fila is saying. I just asked: At the point that -- did his government at any point take any steps to prosecute people? I'm not sure what Mr. Fila's point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understood you. But you have the government holding a meeting, you have the government which met on the 20th of November, 1991, in VELEPROMET. In that government, Slavko Dokmanovic was Minister of Agriculture. Then you have the other government, and Goran Hadzic was President -- Prime Minister. Then you have the government of the Srpska Krajina where Slavko Dokmanovic was not a Minister but Goran Hadzic was Prime Minister of that government too. And then you have a third government which allowed the exhumation at Ovcara, and Goran was the Prime Minister once again of that third government and Dokmanovic was not Minister. Does that make -- have I made myself clear? So when you ask what the government of Goran Hadzic took -- what steps it took, I'm interested in knowing which one of the three governments you have in mind: The first, where Mr. Dokmanovic was a Minister, or some other government, subsequent government? Does that make it clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hadzic. Let me ask you, first of all: At any point in time, in any of these governments that you were associated with, were any steps taken to prosecute people for war crimes against Croats in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Of all the people that committed crimes in the territory under our competency, we always initiated procedure, both in Baranja and Slavonia. And while Slavko Dokmanovic was Minister in that first government, I, as the Prime Minister -- and nobody from the government knew about this, and I don't even now know who was responsible for the Ovcara affair, but I know who was not guilty, who was not guilty, and that is the man sitting here amongst us today. He is quite definitely not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, how can you make that statement if you say you don't know who was guilty? How can you say that he was not guilty?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I know 100 percent that he was not guilty because when -- at the time that he is being accused of this, he was physically not there. He could not have been there physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you with him physically at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was with him until 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you don't know where he was after 3.00 p.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that until this particular trial and proceedings, but in contacts with witnesses, I learned that he was constantly with somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you have been talking to other witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In the case I talked informally, not here but there, because after Dokmanovic's imprisonment, we discussed the matter, and everybody was quite clear on the fact that Slavko could not have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, on the evening of the 27th of June of 1997, after you found out about Mr. Dokmanovic's arrest, you fled from Eastern Slavonia in a boat across the Danube into Serbia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You did not --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That is a lie. I heard that announced on Croatian semi-official news. With my son in my car, I crossed Erdut and I went to Novi Sad. I did not flee and I'm not afraid of the Croats. I hope that they will bring to trial those who are guilty as I am more afraid of those who -- grudges of other kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But it is a fact that you left on the same day of Mr. Dokmanovic's arrest; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That is a fact which has nothing to do with it. It can have something to do with it and need not have. It's got nothing to do with it. It does not say anything of itself, if my son, who is a minor and lives in Novi Sad, and I myself left for Novi Sad. That is a fact in itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the fact that another member of your November 1991 government had been arrested had nothing to do with your decision to leave your lifetime home?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I always lived in Pacetin, but because of integration of this region into Croatia, I do not wish to live in Croatia, and I left Croatia for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it was just a coincidence that it happened on the same evening after Mr. Dokmanovic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I were to follow your logic and to think about matters according to your logic, then the indictment against Dokmanovic, he came back voluntarily to Croatia, which means that he is not guilty; and according to your logic, if I fled, that would mean that I was guilty. I am speaking -- I am saying this following on from your logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm asking you: It's just a coincidence then?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It could have been a coincidence and it need not have been a coincidence. I don't know how somebody else's mind works, particularly those who do not know the problems inherent in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking about someone else's mind, I'm asking you about your own mind. Now, I suppose that it was also a coincidence --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That is why I said it. I don't know how your mind works, and I don't know why -- I did not know why Slavko was arrested and what the charges brought against him were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And so it was also just a coincidence that these 200 men were held at the JNA barracks while your government deliberated; when your government meeting finishes, they are then taken to Ovcara and killed? That was pure coincidence and had nothing to do with what went on at your meeting at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Those are tendentious conclusions. I am sorry about those men that died. I tell you that one day previously, we decided to come to Vukovar, and the fact that something happened apart from this is not our fault. We did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: And you can call that a coincidence, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know in what way the Prosecution is deducing the conclusion that at the same time that the government meeting was held and that people were held in the barracks, whereas witnesses say that that was not the case. The witnesses brought forward by Mr. Williamson. So this is an erroneous conclusion, according to all the systems of the world. I did not raise any objections when he asked his questions -- he's free to ask anything he wants -- but let him ask the truth, if you say that it is the object of us to ascertain the truth. Before 2.00 p.m., the buses were at Ovcara. Both witnesses have testified to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object. If Mr. Fila has questions, he should ask them, but if this is his closing argument then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The argument is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think Mr. Williamson is right. These are your views, your arguments. Have you got any questions to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have a question for the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Fila

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he leave the same day when Dokmanovic was arrested? Did he leave his place of residence on the same day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you leave, move out of Pacetin, your native town? Not just left for Novi Sad, but did you move out, everybody leave, your children, your wife --

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Half the population moved out, and 30.000 Serbs left the district, and that is something we should know here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, they do. The question is: Did you move out because of Slavko Dokmanovic's arrest, the same day, or did you go to Novi Sad with your son as you would have anyway?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As I did on previous occasions, but I moved out definitely because of the policy waged against the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But not on that particular day. You did not pick up your things and leave and move out on that particular day. Do you know whether some buses were in front of the JNA barracks while you were holding your government meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't hear that. Interruptions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you heard -- can you hear me? Will you answer the question once again? You first heard of this for the first time at this trial?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this trial held here today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't hear. I'm sorry, it's interrupted speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us repeat once again slowly: You maintain that you heard of this for the first time, that is, that the buses left the barracks for Ovcara, you have heard that for the first time here today at this trial?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not essential. The essential point is that people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Up to now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Fila repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the buses were in front of the army barracks on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, would you help us with this, please? The meeting on the 20th of November you said was attended by the Lieutenant Colonel, and you said that the Lieutenant Colonel spoke about the prisoners of war. Can you help us as to what he said about the prisoners of war at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do everything to try and help you. The Lieutenant Colonel said that the prisoners of war were a problem of the Yugoslav People's Army and that he does not recognise any of our courts and that we have no competences there, which was, in actual fact, the case, and that was everything that was said about the prisoners of war. What we discussed were the bread supplies and the civilian situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You told us that you advocated a fair trial for them, to say that nothing bad would happen to them. Was that at the meeting or was it later that you advocated that?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: For this -- I advocate this attitude right from the very day that I was born. And during the events that we're talking about, about the 20th, I did not know that something bad was being -- got ready for some individuals, but we just discussed the possible problems that could arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you may assist us in clarifying a few points which you touched upon in your testimony. I understand from what you said before that you, as the Prime Minister or President of the government, convened the meeting of the government for the 20th of November at Vukovar. So how did you get in touch or who told the Lieutenant Colonel of the JNA who attended the meeting? How was he, in a way, asked to participate in this meeting? By whom?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They did not know that this meeting would be held because it was not officially convened. It was a -- and the Lieutenant Colonel happened to be there, and we heard that the commander of the town of Vukovar was there, and then we had the meeting in that way because we thought that it was somebody with the necessary competences. But as I said, he was head of the background formations. That is all that we saw in Vukovar of the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly when you said that the meeting which lasted for about one hour was chaired by the Lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, the Lieutenant Colonel and myself sat up at the rostrum, but as I saw --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is intermittent speech.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: But later on, I stepped down to sit with the Ministers. So the meeting did not have an official character. I did not chair it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Didn't you find it odd that the meeting was being chaired not by you, the Prime Minister or President of the government -- after all, it was a meeting of the government -- but by somebody who did not belong to the government, namely a Lieutenant Colonel of the JNA? Did you complain about that or did you say anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't -- no meeting of the government was held. We just gathered together --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is very difficult to follow. It's intermittent speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We found ourselves -- we met to talk. It was not a government meeting. It was not an official formal government meeting. We just met to discuss matters. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And you said in response to the question put by Judge May that the Lieutenant Colonel spoke of the POWs, the prisoners of war, and their sort. Did he also address the issue of what to do with the civilians who had been taken prisoner, civilians, not armed people, not combatants, those civilians who had been taken prisoner by the occupying army, by the JNA or other people?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The JNA at the time could not have been an occupying army because it was still Yugoslav territory, and when we discussed the prisoners of war, we did not divide them into military or civilian. They were civilians but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They offered resistance. We did not have any competency to decide upon their fate. But we saw them, part of them were in the VELEPROMET warehouse. I heard that they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't hear who was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please specify who was there because we didn't hear part of your reply. You were talking of people who were at VELEPROMET. Who was at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Some civilians, Serbs and Croats, a large group of people. I don't know everybody who was there. I recognised a young boy who was from my village, and I said hello to him, but I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. So to go back again to what the Lieutenant Colonel said. You pointed out that he did not refer to combatants or non-combatants taken prisoner, but generally speaking, to all those who had been detained by the JNA, whether they were civilians or people fighting, armed and fighting as combatants; did he refer to both categories? I'm speaking of people detained by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not very much was mentioned. It was a sort of collective group because we were not able to determine who the actual people were. Some sort of procedure would have been necessary to determine this. And it is the court, up to the court, to determine matters of this kind, as you are doing here today, here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, at one point you said before that, and I quote your words: "Anybody fighting against the Croats was part of the JNA," when a question was put to you about the role of the paramilitary. So do you say that anybody fighting against the Croats was part of the JNA? Do you mean to say by that that all those people, including paramilitary units fighting against the Croats, were under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I answered a concrete question posed to me by the Prosecutor, and I talked about the people that I knew were under the command of the JNA. But under the command and under the control, is that the same thing? I don't think it is the same thing, to be under the command or under the control. But they had nothing to do with the government; that is one thing that I can maintain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, when a question was put to you about why you were wearing a military uniform, you said, and I quote your words: You were wearing a military uniform "to be different from the other people in the area." Could you please elaborate on this particular point? Why did you feel that it was necessary for you to be different from the other people in the area? Just a point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It seems to me that there was a mistranslation. I wore the uniform not to be different from the people in the area, because everybody wore uniforms and that's why I wore a uniform too. So that was one of the reasons. And I mentioned the other ones, so that I could change my clothes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. You are right. Probably I got it wrong. Yes, yes. You probably said not to be different from the other people in the area. Why were you keen not to be different from the other people in the area? Because I understand that quite a few people were wearing civilian clothes, including a witness who testified before you this afternoon and who also attended the meeting of the government in Vukovar, at VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the possibilities. I bought that uniform, and it is the question of my political assessment at that time, whether it was better for me to appear in front of the people in a uniform and to have positive reactions towards the government in that way because I think that at that time, had I worn a tie and a suit, as I am wearing now, I couldn't have done the little I managed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that -- I mean, the fact of wearing a uniform gave you authority and conveyed to other people the idea that you were a person who was wielding power and the authority of a Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. That is not what I am trying to say. It is the opposite, as a matter of fact. On the uniform, I didn't have any insignia, and I wanted to show the people that I was the same as them but that I did hold the post of Prime Minister, but that they could not see on the basis of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question which is a minor question. We saw on a videotape that during the meeting you went out a couple of times, or at least once, to give an interview to a foreign reporter. Do you remember who this foreign reporter was to whom you gave an interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJLSLAV STANIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. Although I saw the picture, I can't remember. I can't remember. As if I had never seen him in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand there is no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Goran Hadzic, thank you for testifying. You may now be released. (Witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we recess, just very briefly, I failed to enter those exhibits that we misplaced, so I would like at this time to tender the video as Prosecutor's Exhibit 205, the transcript in Serb as 205A, and the transcript in English as 205B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there is no objection from Mr. Fila. They are admitted in evidence. I think we should now take our recess, and we will start again tomorrow at 9.30. I understand we have to stop at 11.00 sharp, or even five to 11.00, so that Mr. Fila may meet the members of the ACBQ. I saw on a programme that tomorrow you have a meeting with people from New York, from 11.00 to 11.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was the day after tomorrow. It's on Wednesday, to the best of my knowledge. The day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But we don't have to interrupt the proceedings because my colleague will stay on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Wonderful. All right. So we will resume tomorrow at 9.30 sharp.
